claims.text: A rapid, synchronized thermal pulse causes nearly simultaneous reduction of noble-metal precursors.
Uniform nucleation governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under rapid pulsed heating.
Uniform nucleation minimizes elemental segregation.
Uniform nucleation produces a homogeneous alloy structure.
Rapid synchronized heating enhances surface-atom exposure.
Millisecond-scale pulsed heating triggers simultaneous reduction of the metal precursors.
Uniform nucleation results in an intimate nanoscale mixture of metal atoms.
A narrow thermal window forces all metal precursors to reduce nearly simultaneously.
Synchronized reduction maximizes atomic intermixing.
Greater atomic intermixing suppresses elemental segregation and phase separation.
Differing precursor-reduction kinetics under slower heating cause elemental segregation and phase separation.
Relative to conventional slow heating, rapid pulsed heating produces a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
Relative to conventional slow heating, rapid pulsed heating produces greater surface-atom exposure.
Relative to conventional slow heating, rapid pulsed heating reduces separate-phase formation and elemental segregation.
A slower temperature ramp permits sequential reduction of the metal precursors.
Sequential reduction under the baseline produces noticeable elemental segregation or separate phases.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal precursors with comparable oxidation states and reduction potentials under an inert atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to systems containing non-noble metals.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when precursor reduction kinetics differ greatly.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when scale-up prevents spatially uniform rapid heating.
